posts.text:
A worthwhile (and unnerving) reminder from Anthropic that we should be paying attention to AI ability thresholds, not just steady climbs

In this case, the threshold is the capability needed for a self-replicating AI worm on IoT devices like off-brand TVs www.anthropic.com/research/sel...
posts.meaning: Mollick highlights an Anthropic warning to focus on sudden AI ability thresholds rather than steady capability climbs, citing a threshold involving self-replicating AI worms on IoT devices. Developers and safety researchers care about identifying such critical capability jumps.

posts.text:
Do early adopters win?

Fabric comes: Power BI is over.
Conversational BI: Dashboards and reports are dead.
Claude dashboards: Was conversational BI a thing?

Calm down.

As a professional, you want to stay up to date.
As a company, FOMO bleeds money.

Be ready; don't rush.
posts.meaning: Russo advises professionals and companies to stay updated on tools like Microsoft Fabric and conversational BI without panicking over rapid technology cycles or bleeding money from FOMO. Data professionals can benefit from balancing readiness with measured adoption.

posts.text:
GPT-4 was the undisputed best model in the world for a full year and we all debated whether anyone could catch up or if OpenAI had some secret formula that nobody else knew about.

Now there are are 19 AI models that can run on a modern smartphone that are better than GPT-4!
posts.meaning: Mollick notes that while GPT-4 was the top model for a year, there are now 19 smartphone-capable AI models that outperform it. This illustrates rapid progress in edge and small language models that builders can leverage.

posts.text:
If you announce a model's benchmarks without releasing it (weights, product, api, etc "later"), feels like almost a sure thing that someone releases a better model in your category before you get it out.

... Gemini Argon, Reflection Beam, who's next on this list?
posts.meaning: Lambert argues that announcing model benchmarks without immediate availability means competitors will likely release a better model first. Developers should watch launch strategies closely.

posts.text:
If you haven’t made sure to turn on two-factor authentication on all accounts, have passwords with family in case you get voice calls asking for money, etc, now would be a good time.

AI gains mean the costs of mass targeting individuals with very sophisticated attacks are dropping.
posts.meaning: Mollick warns that AI tools make sophisticated targeted attacks cheaper, advising users to enable two-factor authentication and establish family verification passwords.

posts.text: GPT-6 Pro finds supposed errors in academic papers all the time, just as part of other work. Confirming the errors aren't nitpicks & learning their importance would still take a lot of time today, but it will get faster. We don't have the right mechanisms in place to deal a flood of corrections.
posts.meaning: Mollick notes that AI models frequently spot errors in academic papers, but researchers lack efficient mechanisms to handle the resulting flood of corrections.

posts.text:
As a researcher who did early some work on the productivity impacts of AI chatbots using RCTs, I’d note a lack of similar studies since the dawn of true agents last fall

Partially that is newness & partially research design challenges, but I suspect we are missing some large & important effects

posts.text:
Anyhow, I think we are now done with the last round of skeptical responses to AI after Navier-Stokes. Yes, AI is now capable of producing novel proofs to hard problems that have eluded us

The next line will be that this is only constrained to math because of RL training. I suspect not, we will see.
posts.meaning: Mollick claims AI is now capable of producing novel proofs to hard problems, suggesting skepticism regarding math constraints is ending.

posts.text:
When people talk about AI easily replacing workers, I think about this ethnography of copier repair technicians in the 1990s.

Reading it, you see how work is complicated and improvised by workers and informal and badly documented.

(But eventually technology did largely eliminate this job)
posts.meaning: Mollick compares AI workplace replacement fears to historical studies of copier repair technicians, noting that while work is often improvised and poorly documented, technology eventually eliminates those jobs.

posts.text:
After a brief but institution-eroding slop science era, it increasingly looks like we are going to have 2 revolutions from AI:
1) Everything ever published will be re-read and re-judged in ways that human scientists never anticipated
2) Novel discoveries will start to come faster than we can absorb
posts.meaning: Mollick argues that AI will drive two major revolutions: enabling the re-evaluation of all published science in unforeseen ways, and accelerating novel discoveries past our capacity to absorb them.

posts.text: Big swing happening from this summer's trend to have AI running on virtual machines on your own computer (Claude and ChatGPT apps) to moving them back into you having a dedicated VM the cloud (Claude Cowork just announced they were doing this, also Grok Bot, Dot, and others). posts.text: Reflection joins the list of Nvidia and Thinking Machines who have tried to release their strongest models and come up behind Chinese counterparts. There's a lot of ways people will overthink this, but the clearest takeaway should be that the Chinese are very very good at building LLMs.
posts.meaning: Lambert notes that several labs have released strong models that fall behind Chinese counterparts, demonstrating that Chinese developers are exceptionally skilled at building LLMs.

posts.text:
AI policy right now, especially from the Labs, makes me think of this poem.

If you believe superintelligence is near, you don't need to make hard decisions about how to build AI to make the world better. Just wait for ASI & it will decide for us, for better or worse. But if that doesn't happen...
posts.meaning: Mollick criticizes current AI lab policies, suggesting that belief in near-term superintelligence lets labs avoid making hard present-day decisions about building better AI.
